planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Tanaka is a large-fruited, late-ripening Japanese loquat cultivar that extends the loquat season past earlier varieties like Advance and Champagne.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Tanaka is a classic Japanese loquat cultivar, long regarded as a benchmark variety in Japanese and California loquat breeding for its large, rounded, russet-orange fruit and firm, sweet, mildly tangy flesh. It ripens later than most other loquat cultivars — typically extending the harvest into late spring — which makes it a valuable companion to earlier-ripening selections for growers wanting a longer fresh-loquat season. The fruit holds well on the tree without over-softening, giving some flexibility in harvest timing compared to more delicate cultivars. Trees are vigorous and moderately cold-hardy for a subtropical fruit, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s°F once established, though open flowers and young fruit are damaged by hard freezes — plant in a warm microclimate in zone 8 for the most reliable crops. Thin heavy fruit clusters to two or three fruits per cluster shortly after fruit set to improve individual fruit size.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mogi is a historically important, smaller-fruited Japanese loquat cultivar that has been grown and bred from for well over a century.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mogi is one of the oldest and most historically significant Japanese loquat cultivars, originating from Nagasaki and serving as a parent or foundation selection behind many later loquat cultivars developed in Japan and California. Fruit is smaller and rounder than modern large-fruited selections, with pale orange, juicy, sweet-tart flesh and a thin skin. Though newer cultivars have surpassed Mogi in fruit size, it remains valued by collectors and heritage-fruit growers for its productivity, reliability, and historic significance in loquat breeding. Trees bloom in fall and fruit ripens in spring, so protect open flowers and developing fruit from hard freezes with row cover during cold snaps in zone 8, where loquat is at the edge of its reliable range. Established trees tolerate heat, drought, and a range of soil types well, needing only routine care once past the first two years.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Gerardi Dwarf stays compact enough for a large container or small garden bed while still producing full-sized, full-flavored mulberries, and it is self-fertile so a single plant will fruit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Gerardi Dwarf is a naturally compact mulberry selection that stays a fraction of the size of standard mulberry trees — often kept as low as 3–6 feet with pruning — while still producing full-sized, sweet, juicy dark berries typical of good mulberry cultivars, making it one of the few mulberries genuinely practical for a small yard, large container, or spot under bird netting. It is self-fertile, so a single plant fruits without a pollinator, and its small stature allows the whole canopy to be netted against birds, which is otherwise the biggest challenge in mulberry growing since ripening fruit is intensely attractive to them. Prune annually in late winter to maintain the compact form and to encourage a flush of new fruiting wood, since mulberries fruit on both old and new growth. Harvest by gently shaking ripe branches over a sheet or tarp, since ripe mulberries detach easily and bruise if hand-picked one at a time; fruit ripens over several weeks rather than all at once, extending the harvest season.

common_name: Meech's Prolific Quince (Classic American Heirloom Quince)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, and Meech's Prolific bears young and heavily, true to its name.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Meech's Prolific is a nineteenth-century American heirloom quince, long documented in historic US pomology references as one of the heaviest-bearing and most reliable quince cultivars available, producing large, bright golden-yellow, intensely fragrant fruit prized for preserves, jelly, paste, and baking. As the name suggests, it is notably precocious and prolific, often bearing well within just a few years of planting and continuing to crop dependably year after year. Like all quince the fruit is hard and astringent raw and is meant to be cooked, which transforms the pale flesh to a rosy pink and develops the complex floral-honey flavor quince is prized for. Prune in late winter to an open vase form for good air circulation, which is the best defense against fire blight, the primary disease risk for quince in humid regions. Harvest in fall once fruit has turned fully golden and developed its characteristic strong perfume; quince stores well in a cool location for weeks after picking.

common_name: Portugal Quince (Large Highly Aromatic Heirloom Quince)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, though Portugal is a shier bearer than some other quince cultivars and benefits from a warm, sheltered site.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, ideally in a warm, sheltered spot; Portugal is an old European heirloom quince long grown in American heritage orchards, prized above most other quince cultivars for its very large, intensely aromatic fruit and, uniquely among quinces, flesh that cooks down to a rosy-red color with a smoother, less gritty texture than most quince varieties — traditionally considered the finest quince for jelly and paste making. It is a somewhat shier, slower bearer than heavier-cropping cultivars like Meech's Prolific or Orange, and performs best with a warm site and attentive care in its early years, but the exceptional fruit quality has kept it in cultivation for centuries despite more productive alternatives. As with all quince, fruit is hard and astringent raw and must be cooked to develop its rich, honeyed, floral flavor. Prune to an open form for good air circulation to reduce fire blight risk, and harvest in fall once fruit turns golden-yellow and is strongly fragrant.
